title: Augmentin and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Augmentin?
excerpt: Can you drink on Augmentin? Why amoxicillin-clavulanate has no direct alcohol reaction, but how alcohol worsens its stomach side effects, its rare liver risk, and when to wait.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Augmentin? How alcohol affects its diarrhea and nausea, the rare Augmentin liver risk, how long to wait, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Augmentin and alcohol don't have a known direct drug interaction. A drink won't stop the antibiotic working, and it won't set off the violent flushing-and-vomiting reaction that a few other antibiotics are famous for. But Augmentin is not just amoxicillin. It also contains **clavulanate**, and that extra ingredient brings two problems that alcohol can make worse: a high rate of stomach upset and diarrhea, and a rare but real risk of drug-induced liver injury. So the practical answer is more cautious than it is for plain amoxicillin. A single drink is unlikely to hurt a healthy adult, but most people feel better and recover more smoothly if they skip alcohol until the course is done.

**The quick rules:** Take each Augmentin dose at the start of a meal. Skip alcohol if you have diarrhea, nausea, a fever, or feel properly ill. Don't drink heavily at any point during the course. If you drink three or more drinks most days, or you have liver disease, tell your prescriber before you start. Never skip, delay, or double a dose because you've been drinking, and finish the course unless your doctor says otherwise. Watch for yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or itching for a few weeks after you finish, because the rare liver reaction can show up late.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your antibiotic and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on Augmentin if** you drink most days, have liver disease or have had liver problems on an antibiotic before, are over 65, take more than one antibiotic, or are also taking a prescription painkiller. **Get medical help right away if** you have trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, a widespread or blistering rash, severe or bloody diarrhea, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Augmentin Actually Is

Augmentin is a brand name for **amoxicillin-clavulanate** (also called co-amoxiclav in the UK and elsewhere). It's two drugs in one tablet:

1. **Amoxicillin**, a penicillin-type antibiotic that kills bacteria by breaking down their cell walls.
2. **Clavulanate (clavulanic acid)**, which doesn't kill much on its own. Its job is to block an enzyme called beta-lactamase that some bacteria use to destroy amoxicillin. With clavulanate on board, amoxicillin can reach bacteria it would otherwise miss.

That's why doctors reach for Augmentin when plain amoxicillin might not be enough: stubborn sinus infections, some ear infections, animal and human bites, dental abscesses, certain skin infections, some pneumonias, and some urinary infections.

The second ingredient is what makes this page different from our guide to [amoxicillin and alcohol](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol). Plain amoxicillin is one of the gentler antibiotics. Augmentin is harder on the gut, and it carries a liver warning that amoxicillin alone mostly doesn't.

## Is There a Direct Interaction Between Augmentin and Alcohol?

No significant one is known. Here's what that means in plain terms.

**No disulfiram-like reaction.** A few antibiotics, mainly metronidazole and tinidazole, are linked to a reaction with alcohol that causes flushing, a pounding headache, vomiting, and a racing heart. Doctors call it "disulfiram-like" because it resembles the effect of the anti-drinking drug Antabuse. Neither amoxicillin nor clavulanate is known to cause this. You can read more about which antibiotics do in our [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol).

**No change in how the drug works.** Amoxicillin and clavulanate are mostly cleared by the kidneys, not broken down by the liver enzymes that alcohol affects. A moderate amount of alcohol doesn't lower their levels or stop them killing bacteria.

**No alcohol warning on the label like the strict ones.** The Augmentin prescribing information doesn't list alcohol as a drug interaction the way the metronidazole label does.

So if you had a glass of wine with dinner and then remembered you were on Augmentin, there's no reason to panic. The concerns below are about side effects stacking up and about the liver, not about a dangerous reaction at the table.

## Problem One: Augmentin Is Hard on the Gut, and So Is Alcohol

If you've taken Augmentin before, you may already know this one. Diarrhea, loose stools, nausea, and stomach discomfort are among its most common side effects, and they're noticeably more common than with plain amoxicillin. The clavulanate component is the main reason. Higher clavulanate doses are linked with more stomach trouble, which is one reason different Augmentin strengths aren't interchangeable.

There are two things going on:

- **Direct gut irritation.** Clavulanate itself seems to speed up the gut and irritate it, which explains why some people get loose stools within a day or two of starting.
- **Disrupted gut bacteria.** Like most antibiotics, Augmentin also knocks back the normal bacteria in your intestines. That can cause diarrhea, bloating, and, less often, a yeast infection.

Now add alcohol. Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and intestines, increases stomach acid, and speeds up how quickly things move through your bowel. That's why many people get loose stools after a night of drinking even without any medicine involved. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains why. Put the two together and you're asking a gut that's already irritated by the antibiotic to deal with a second irritant.

The result usually isn't dangerous, but it's unpleasant: more diarrhea, more cramping, more nausea, and a higher chance of dehydration. Dehydration is the part that can turn a bad day into a worse one, especially if you're also running a fever.

### How to make Augmentin easier on your stomach

- **Take it at the start of a meal.** The Augmentin label specifically advises this. It reduces stomach upset, and it also helps your body absorb the clavulanate properly.
- **Drink water, not alcohol.** If you have loose stools, replace fluids steadily.
- **Eat plain food if your stomach is unsettled.** Rice, toast, bananas, and soups are easier going than greasy or spicy food.
- **Ask about probiotics.** Some research reviews have found that certain probiotics may lower the chance of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, though results vary by product and the evidence isn't settled. If you try one, ask your pharmacist about spacing it a couple of hours away from your Augmentin dose.

## When Diarrhea on Augmentin Is Serious: C. difficile

This is the warning that matters most, because people sometimes blame it on drinking and wait too long.

Any antibiotic can allow a bacterium called **Clostridioides difficile** (C. diff) to overgrow in the gut. It causes a more serious form of diarrhea that can lead to severe colon inflammation. The Augmentin label, like most antibiotic labels, carries a warning about it. It can start during the course or **up to two months after you finish**.

**Call a doctor promptly if you have:**

- Watery diarrhea three or more times a day for more than a day or two
- Diarrhea with blood or mucus
- Diarrhea with fever, bad stomach cramps, or a tender, swollen belly
- Diarrhea that starts after the course ended and doesn't settle

Don't take anti-diarrhea medicine like loperamide for this kind of diarrhea without checking with a doctor first. And don't assume it's from last night's drinks. Ordinary post-drinking diarrhea settles within a day once you stop drinking. C. diff doesn't.

## Problem Two: Augmentin and Your Liver

This is the part most "can I drink on antibiotics" articles skip, and it's the main reason Augmentin deserves more care than plain amoxicillin.

### What the evidence says

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is one of the drugs most often linked to **drug-induced liver injury**. In large registries that track liver injury caused by medicines in the US and Europe, it consistently appears at or near the top of the list. That sounds alarming, so it's worth putting in context: Augmentin is also one of the most widely prescribed antibiotics in the world, and the reaction is rare for any one person. Most people take it with no liver problems at all.

The Augmentin label warns about hepatic dysfunction, including hepatitis and **cholestatic jaundice**. "Cholestatic" means bile backs up in the liver instead of draining normally, which causes yellowing, itching, and dark urine. The label notes that this reaction:

- Has been reported more often in **older adults, men, and people taking it for longer courses**
- Can start **during treatment or several weeks after** the last dose
- Is **usually reversible**, though in rare cases it has been severe

The clavulanate component is thought to be the main driver, since plain amoxicillin is linked to liver injury far less often. The reaction is described as "idiosyncratic," meaning it depends on how a particular person's body and immune system respond rather than simply on taking too much. Some research has tied it to certain inherited immune system gene types, which helps explain why it hits a small number of people and not others.

### Where alcohol fits in

Here's the honest version: **there is no good evidence that a drink or two triggers Augmentin liver injury.** This isn't like Tylenol, where alcohol changes how the drug is broken down and tips the liver toward a toxic by-product. (Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains that mechanism.)

But there are still good reasons to be careful:

- **Two stressors on one organ.** Heavy drinking stresses the liver on its own. If your liver is also reacting to Augmentin, adding regular heavy drinking is the wrong direction.
- **Existing liver problems.** People with fatty liver disease, hepatitis, or a history of liver injury from Augmentin start with less margin. The label says Augmentin should be used with caution in people with liver impairment and that people who had liver problems on it before shouldn't take it again.
- **Confusing symptoms.** Early liver trouble can show up as tiredness, nausea, and losing your appetite, which are easy to blame on a hangover or on the infection. Drinking during the course makes it harder to notice when something's actually wrong.

If you drink three or more drinks most days, or have any liver condition, tell the person prescribing Augmentin. They may still prescribe it, choose a different antibiotic, or suggest a blood test. That's a conversation for them, not a guess for you.

### Warning signs of liver trouble

Call your doctor promptly if any of these show up during the course or in the weeks after:

- Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
- Dark, tea-colored urine or pale stools
- Itching all over without a rash
- Pain or tenderness under the right side of your ribs
- Unusual tiredness, nausea, or loss of appetite that doesn't fit a hangover or the infection

Because the reaction can appear after you've finished the pills, it's worth keeping these in mind for a few weeks, especially if you're older or had a long course.

## Does Alcohol Make Augmentin Less Effective?

Not directly. A moderate amount of alcohol doesn't stop amoxicillin-clavulanate from working. But drinking can undermine treatment in practical ways:

- **Missed or late doses.** Augmentin is usually taken every 8 or 12 hours. A late night out is a common reason a dose gets forgotten or taken hours late. Steady levels matter for antibiotics.
- **Vomited doses.** If you throw up soon after taking a dose, some of it may not have been absorbed. Ask your pharmacist whether to repeat it rather than guessing.
- **Your immune system does part of the job.** The antibiotic knocks bacteria back, but your body finishes the work. Heavy drinking can disrupt sleep, dehydrate you, and dampen immune responses for a while. Our guide to [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) explains how.

So alcohol rarely "cancels" Augmentin. It just makes it more likely that the course goes less smoothly than it should.

## Augmentin and Alcohol: Common Situations

### Augmentin for a tooth infection

Dentists often prescribe Augmentin for abscesses and other dental infections. Augmentin itself doesn't react with alcohol, but two things often come along with it:

- **Metronidazole.** For some gum and tooth infections, dentists add or switch to metronidazole. That one carries a strict warning: no alcohol during the course and for at least three days after. If you were given two antibiotics, check both names.
- **Painkillers.** After dental work you may be taking ibuprofen, acetaminophen, or a prescription opioid. Opioids and alcohol together can dangerously slow breathing, and acetaminophen plus heavy drinking is hard on the liver. Our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers that one.

### Augmentin for a sinus or ear infection

These are some of the most common reasons people get Augmentin. Alcohol can make nasal congestion and sinus pressure feel worse for some people, because it widens blood vessels in the nose, and it disrupts the sleep you need to recover. If you're also taking a cold or flu product, check whether it contains acetaminophen or a sedating antihistamine, both of which have their own alcohol cautions.

### Augmentin for a bite or skin infection

Animal bites and some skin infections are classic Augmentin uses. Here the bigger issue is the infection itself. If the area gets redder, more swollen, or more painful, or red streaks spread out from it, see a doctor. Don't let a night of drinking delay you noticing that.

### Augmentin XR and the different strengths

Augmentin comes in several strengths and forms, including standard tablets, chewables, liquid suspensions for children, and an extended-release version (Augmentin XR). The alcohol advice is the same across them. One related safety point from the label: the tablets aren't interchangeable just because the amoxicillin adds up. For example, two 250 mg tablets don't equal one 500 mg tablet, because they contain different amounts of clavulanate. Take exactly the tablets you were prescribed.

## How Long After Augmentin Can You Drink?

From a drug-interaction standpoint, there's **no required waiting period**. Amoxicillin and clavulanate both clear the body quickly, typically within about a day of your last dose for most people with normal kidneys.

A more useful way to decide:

1. **Finish the full course.** Stopping early because you feel better can let the infection come back.
2. **Wait until you actually feel well.** No fever, no lingering stomach upset, no diarrhea.
3. **Start light.** One drink with food, not a big night, to see how your stomach handles it.
4. **Keep an eye out for late warning signs.** The rare liver reaction and C. diff diarrhea can both start after the course ends. If you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching, or persistent watery diarrhea, call a doctor and don't drink until you've been checked.

## If You Already Drank on Augmentin

This is a very common worry, and in most cases the answer is reassuring.

- **Don't panic.** One or two drinks on Augmentin is very unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction.
- **Don't skip your next dose.** Take it on schedule, with food.
- **Hydrate.** Water or an electrolyte drink helps, especially if your stomach is unsettled.
- **Expect your gut to complain.** You may get looser stools or more nausea than usual. That usually settles within a day.
- **Get help if something unusual happens.** Severe or bloody diarrhea, a spreading rash, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, or yellowing skin all need medical attention, whether or not alcohol was involved.

If you drank heavily, mention it to your pharmacist or doctor, especially if you have liver disease or are on a long course.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You have more reason to skip alcohol completely while on Augmentin if you:

- Drink **three or more drinks most days**, or binge regularly
- Have **liver disease**, fatty liver, hepatitis, or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- Had **jaundice or liver problems on Augmentin before** (tell your prescriber; the label says not to take it again)
- Are **over 65**, or are on a **longer course** than a week or so
- Already have **diarrhea, vomiting, or a fever**
- Are taking **metronidazole, an opioid painkiller, or a sedating cold medicine** alongside it

For a wider look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Practical Tips If You Do Have a Drink

If your doctor or pharmacist has said a drink is fine, these habits keep the risk low:

1. **Confirm the drug name.** Check the label. "The one for my tooth" might be Augmentin, or it might be metronidazole.
2. **Keep it to one or two.** Not a night out.
3. **Drink with food, and take your dose with a meal.** An empty stomach makes everything worse.
4. **Alternate with water.** Both the antibiotic and alcohol can dehydrate you through diarrhea and extra urination.
5. **Don't let it shift your dosing schedule.** Set a phone reminder if you'll be out.
6. **Stop if your stomach is already upset.** Diarrhea is a sign to skip the drink, not push through.

## What About DHM and Other Supplements?

People who use hangover supplements sometimes ask whether they can keep taking them on an antibiotic. The honest answer is that most supplements, DHM included, haven't been studied alongside amoxicillin-clavulanate. There is no good evidence that DHM protects against Augmentin's stomach side effects or its rare liver reaction, and no supplement makes it a good idea to drink heavily during a course. The simplest approach is to pause new supplements until you've finished, or check with your pharmacist first. That also makes it easier to tell what's causing any side effect you notice.

Once you've finished the course and feel back to normal, DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound some people use around social drinking. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, so it's promising rather than proven. If you want to try it then, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter more than any pill: pacing, food, water, and sleep. If liver health is on your mind, our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) walks through the evidence for each option.

## The Bottom Line

- Augmentin (amoxicillin-clavulanate) has **no known direct interaction** with alcohol and doesn't cause a flushing, vomiting reaction.
- It's **harder on the gut** than plain amoxicillin, and alcohol tends to make the diarrhea and nausea worse. Take each dose at the start of a meal.
- Augmentin is one of the drugs most often linked to **rare drug-induced liver injury**, which can appear during or weeks after the course. There's no good evidence a drink triggers it, but heavy drinking and liver disease are reasons to talk to your prescriber first.
- Severe, watery, or bloody diarrhea, during or after the course, needs a doctor. Don't write it off as a hangover.
- The safest plan: skip alcohol until you've finished the course and feel well, then start light. When in doubt, ask the pharmacist who filled your prescription.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Augmentin?**

Augmentin (amoxicillin-clavulanate) has no known direct chemical interaction with alcohol, so a single light drink is generally considered low risk for a healthy adult. It is still a poor match in practice: Augmentin commonly causes diarrhea and nausea, alcohol makes both worse, and Augmentin is one of the antibiotics most often linked to rare drug-induced liver injury. Most people are better off skipping alcohol until the course is finished and they feel well. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you drink most days or have liver disease.

**Is Augmentin different from amoxicillin when it comes to alcohol?**

Yes, in two practical ways. Augmentin adds clavulanate, which makes stomach upset and diarrhea more common than with plain amoxicillin, and alcohol irritates the same gut. Augmentin is also much more strongly associated with rare drug-induced liver injury than amoxicillin on its own. Neither drug causes a flushing, vomiting reaction with alcohol the way metronidazole can.

**How long after finishing Augmentin can I drink alcohol?**

There is no required waiting period from a drug-interaction standpoint, and the drug itself clears the body within about a day of the last dose. A sensible approach is to wait until your infection has cleared, your stomach has settled, and any diarrhea has stopped, then start with one drink rather than a big night. Because the rare Augmentin liver reaction can appear days to weeks after the course ends, watch for yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching, or pain under the right ribs, and call a doctor if they appear.

**Will alcohol stop Augmentin from working?**

A moderate amount of alcohol does not stop amoxicillin-clavulanate from killing bacteria. Drinking can still get in the way indirectly: a late night can mean a missed or delayed dose, vomiting can bring a dose back up, and heavy drinking can disrupt sleep and immune function while your body is fighting the infection. If you vomit soon after a dose, ask your pharmacist whether to repeat it.

**Can Augmentin and alcohol damage your liver?**

Augmentin can, rarely, cause liver injury on its own. It is one of the drugs most often named in drug-induced liver injury registries in the US and Europe, and the label warns about hepatitis and jaundice that can start during treatment or several weeks after. There is no good evidence that a drink or two triggers this reaction, but adding regular heavy drinking puts extra strain on a liver that may be under stress. If you drink heavily most days or have liver disease, tell your prescriber before starting Augmentin.

**Why do I have diarrhea on Augmentin, and does alcohol make it worse?**

Diarrhea is one of the most common Augmentin side effects. The clavulanate part irritates the gut, and the antibiotic also disrupts the normal gut bacteria. Alcohol speeds up how fast food moves through your gut and irritates its lining, so it usually makes antibiotic diarrhea worse. Taking each dose at the start of a meal helps. Severe, watery, or bloody diarrhea, especially with fever or cramps, can be a C. difficile infection and needs a doctor, even if it starts after the course ends.

**Can I drink on Augmentin for a tooth infection?**

Augmentin itself doesn't react with alcohol, but dental infections often come with other medicines that do matter. Dentists sometimes add metronidazole, which carries a strict no-alcohol warning during the course and for three days after. Prescription painkillers after dental work, especially opioids and products containing acetaminophen, are also a bad mix with alcohol. Check every medicine name you were given before you drink.

**Does DHM help if I drink while on Augmentin?**

There's no good evidence that DHM protects against Augmentin side effects or its rare liver reaction, and it hasn't been studied alongside amoxicillin-clavulanate. It's simplest to skip new supplements during the course, or check with your pharmacist first. DHM is a plant compound some people use around social drinking once they're healthy again, and most of its research comes from animal and lab studies with limited human data.
